title: A different calling from the robber’s
source_text: Οὐκ ἐπὶ μυστήρια οὖν καὶ κοινωνίαν σοφίας „ἐν μυστηρίῳ“ ἀποκεκρυμμένης, „ἣν προώρισεν ὁ θεὸς πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων εἰς δόξαν“ τῶν δικαίων ἑαυτοῦ, καλοῦμεν τὸν ἄδικον καὶ κλέπτην καὶ τοιχωρύχον καὶ φαρμακέα καὶ ἱερόσυλον καὶ τυμβωρύχον καὶ ὅσους ἂν ἄλλους δεινοποιῶν ὁ Κέλσος ὀνομάσαι, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ θεραπείαν, ἔστι γὰρ ἐν τῇ τοῦ λόγου θειότητι ἄλλα μὲν τὰ θεραπευτικὰ τῶν „κακῶς“ ἐχόντων βοηθήματα, περὶ ὧν εἶπεν ὁ λόγος τό· „οὐ χρείαν ἔχουσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατροῦ ἀλλ᾿ οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες.“ ἄλλα δὲ τὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς ψυχὴν καὶ σῶμα παραδεικνύντα „ἀποκάλυψιν μυστηρίου, χρόνοις αἰωνίοις σεσιγημένου φανερωθέντος δὲ νῦν διά τε γραφῶν προφητικῶν“ καὶ „τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ,“ ἑκάστῳ τῶν τελείων ἐπιφαινομένης καὶ φωτιζούσης εἰς ἀψευδῆ γνῶσιν τῶν πραγμάτων τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ἐπεὶ δὲ δεινοποιῶν τὰ καθ᾿ ἡμῶν ἐγκλήματα ἐπιφέρει οἷς ὠνόμασεν ἐν ἀνθρώποις μιαρωτάτοις τὸ τίνας ἄλλους προκηρύττων λῃστὴς ἐκάλεσε; καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο φήσομεν ὅτι λῃστὴς μὲν τοὺς τοιούτους καλεῖ, χρώμενος αὐτῶν τῇ πονηρίᾳ κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπων, οὓς φονεύειν καὶ συλᾶν βούλεται· Χριστιανὸς δὲ κἂν καλῇ οὓς ὁ λῃστὴς καλεῖ, διάφορον κλῆσιν αὐτοὺς καλεῖ, ἵν᾿ αὐτῶν καταδήσῃ „τὰ τραύματα“ τῷ λόγῳ καὶ ἐπιχέῃ τῇ φλεγμαινούσῃ ἐν κακοῖς ψυχῇ τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου φάρμακα, ἀνάλογον οἴνῳ καὶ ἐλαίῳ καὶ μαλάγματι καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς ἀπὸ ἰατρικῆς ψυχῆς βοηθήμασιν.
pass_a_gloss: Not then to mysteries (μυστήριον) and fellowship (κοινωνία) of wisdom hidden (ἀποκρύπτω) ‘in a mystery’, ‘which God foreordained (προορίζω) before the ages (αἰών) for glory (δόξα)’ of his righteous (δίκαιος) ones, do we call the unjust and thief and housebreaker and poisoner and temple-robber and grave-robber and whatever others Celsus, exaggerating (δεινοποιέω), might name, but to healing (θεραπεία). For there are in the divinity (θειότης) of the Word (λόγος) some healing (θεραπευτικός) aids (βοήθημα) of those faring ‘badly’ (κακῶς ἔχω), about whom the Word said the [saying]: ‘those who are strong (ἰσχύω) have no need (χρεία) of a physician (ἰατρός) but those faring badly’; and other [aids] showing (παραδείκνυμι) to the pure in soul and body ‘revelation (ἀποκάλυψις) of a mystery kept silent (σιγάω) in eternal (αἰώνιος) times, but now made manifest (φανερόω) through prophetic (προφητικός) writings (γραφή)’ and ‘the appearing (ἐπιφάνεια) of our Lord Jesus Christ’, [the appearing] shining upon (ἐπιφαίνομαι) each of the perfect (τέλειος) and enlightening (φωτίζω) to unerring (ἀψευδής) knowledge (γνῶσις) of the realities (πρᾶγμα) the ruling part (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν). And since, exaggerating the charges (ἔγκλημα) against us, he adds (ἐπιφέρω) to those he named among most foul (μιαρός) men the [words] ‘whom else would a robber proclaiming have called?’, to this too we shall say that a robber calls such, using (χράομαι) their wickedness (πονηρία) against men whom he wishes to murder (φονεύω) and rob (συλάω); but a Christian, even if he calls whom the robber calls, calls them a different (διάφορος) calling (κλῆσις), that he may bind up (καταδέω) ‘the wounds (τραῦμα)’ of them with the Word and pour on (ἐπιχέω) the soul inflamed (φλεγμαίνω) in evils the remedies (φάρμακον) from the Word, analogous (ἀνάλογον) to wine (οἶνος) and oil (ἔλαιον) and poultice (μάλαγμα) and the remaining aids from medicine (ἰατρική) of soul.
pass_b_english: It is not, then, to the mysteries and to a share in the wisdom hidden “in a mystery,” “which God foreordained before the ages for the glory” of his righteous ones (1 Corinthians 2:7), that we call the unjust man, the thief, the housebreaker, the poisoner, the temple-robber, the grave-robber, and whatever others Celsus might name in his exaggeration; we call them to healing. For in the divinity of the Word there are, on the one hand, healing remedies for those who are “sick,” about whom the Word said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9:12; Mark 2:17). And there are, on the other, remedies that show to those who are pure in soul and body “the revelation of the mystery that was kept in silence through eternal ages, but is now made manifest through the prophetic writings” (Romans 16:25–26) and through “the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Timothy 6:14; compare 2 Timothy 1:10), an appearing that shines upon each of the perfect and enlightens the ruling part of the soul for an unerring knowledge of things as they are.

But since, exaggerating his charges against us, he adds to those whom he named among the foulest of men the words, “Whom else would a robber summon by public proclamation?”, we shall reply to this as well: A robber calls such people in order to use their wickedness against those whom he wishes to murder and rob. But a Christian, even if he calls those whom the robber calls, calls them with a different calling, so that he may bind up “their wounds” with the Word (Luke 10:34) and pour on the soul inflamed with evils the remedies that come from the Word, which answer to the wine and oil and poultice and the other aids of the medicine of the soul.

choices.choice: 1 Corinthians 2:7 ends ‘for our glory’ (εἰς δόξαν ἡμῶν); Origen writes ‘for the glory of his righteous ones’, so only the words that match are inside quotation marks. Matthew 9:12 and Mark 2:17 both read exactly οὐ χρείαν ἔχουσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατροῦ ἀλλ᾿ οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες (Luke 5:31 has οἱ ὑγιαίνοντες), so both are cited. Romans 16:25–26 is quoted closely. τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ matches 1 Timothy 6:14 word for word, while the thought (a mystery made manifest now through the appearing) is that of 2 Timothy 1:10 (‘our Saviour Christ Jesus’); the first is cited, the second with ‘compare’. τὰ τραύματα … οἴνῳ καὶ ἐλαίῳ takes up the Good Samaritan, Luke 10:34 (κατέδησεν τὰ τραύματα … ἐπιχέων ἔλαιον καὶ οἶνον). μάλαγμα (‘poultice’) together with oil may also recall Isaiah 1:6 LXX; uncertain, not cited inline. ‘The Word’ is capitalised throughout as the divine Logos who heals (ἐν τῇ τοῦ λόγου θειότητι; περὶ ὧν εἶπεν ὁ λόγος, the saying of Jesus). τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, the Stoic ‘ruling part’ of the soul, rendered ‘the ruling part of the soul’. διάφορον κλῆσιν αὐτοὺς καλεῖ keeps the play on καλεῖν/κλῆσις (‘calls them with a different calling’). δεινοποιῶν (twice) rendered ‘in his exaggeration’ and ‘exaggerating’. Celsus’s question is quoted again in double quotation marks, as in 3.59.
δεινοποιῶν (twice): wordy ‘in his effort to make things look dreadful’ / ‘to make his charges look dreadful’ to ‘in his exaggeration’ / ‘exaggerating his charges’; translator note updated
